newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian-U.S. crew rest on Mir after latest crisis.
newsitem.headline: Russian-U.S. crew rest on Mir after latest crisis.

text.p: The weary Russian-U.S. crew on the Mir space station were given a chance to relax on Saturday after dealing with their latest crisis.

Officials at Korolyov Mission Control said only minor repairs were planned during the day for Russians Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin and American Michael Foale after they restored Mir's orientation on Friday.

The Russian official in charge of the mission praised the crew's efforts but suggested they would not be asked to carry out the risky repairs needed to fix their power supply following a collision in orbit on June 25.

"I think it is better for us not to propose to this crew that they go out into open space as there is only a little time until the next expedition and the lads are tired," mission director Vladimir Solovyov told Russia's ORT television.
"They have been through a lot, something which has a serious effect on a person's pyschology."
Mir's power supply was damaged in a collision during a docking manoeuvre on June 25 which punctured the Spektr module attached to the space station.

Problems have since plagued the mission. An unidentified liquid leaked into space, Tsibliyev suffered a heart problem and Mir lost orientation on Thursday when one of the crew pulled out the wrong cable and a computer crashed.

Tsibliyev and Lazutkin had initially been expected to don spacesuits to enter the airless Spektr module to carry out the power supply repairs while Foale, a British-born NASA physicist, waited in an escape capsule.
But Solovyov indicated that the repair work would probably now be left to a crew due to arrive on Mir on August 7.
Two Russian cosmonauts, Pavel Vinogradov and Anatoly Solovyov, are already training outside Moscow at Zvyozdny Gorodok, which is often referred to as Star City, to undertake the repairs.
"The intensive training in Star City showed that some special instruments will be needed to make the repairs safe for the cosmonauts," Solovyov told reporters at Mission Control.
"These instruments can only be delivered by the next space craft and then it will be highly unreasonable to send the weary old crew to do the repairs rather then the fresh new crew."
Solovyov said the space mission of French cosmonaut Leopold Eyharts, who had been due to blast off in the next Soyuz craft with the two Russians on August 5, was sure to be postponed.
"The huge cargo which needs to be taken to the Mir does not allow room for a third person in the Soyuz spacecraft," he said.
Solovyov said the modules where Eyharts was to conduct his experiments had lost power supply after the June 25 collision.
"I believe the French understand that there is no use going to space without a chance to carry out a scientific programme," he said. "We will repair the station and invite the French to come later."
